- Use `Suspense` boundaries for loading states
- Lazy load heavy components with `dynamic()` imports
- Minimize client-side state; prefer server components where possible

### Build & Module Optimization

The project uses several optimizations to reduce module load times:

**Next.js Config** (`next.config.ts`):
- `optimizePackageImports` - Tree-shakes large packages like `lucide-react` (44MB), Radix UI, and `@tiptap/*`
- `serverExternalPackages` - Excludes `pdfkit` from bundling (Turbopack rewrites `__dirname` to `/ROOT/`, breaking font file resolution)
- `transpilePackages` - Better tree-shaking for `@getbrevo/brevo`
- `turbopack` - Faster builds with Next.js 16's default bundler

**Lazy Initialization Patterns**:
- **Brevo SDK** (`src/lib/email.ts`): Uses named imports instead of wildcard (`import * as brevo`), API client lazy-initialized on first use
  ```typescript
  // Good - named imports, lazy init
  import { TransactionalEmailsApi, SendSmtpEmail } from "@getbrevo/brevo";
  let apiInstance: TransactionalEmailsApi | null = null;
  function getApiInstance() { /* create on first call */ }

  // Bad - loads entire SDK at module load
  import * as brevo from "@getbrevo/brevo";
  const apiInstance = new brevo.TransactionalEmailsApi();
  ```
- **Logger** (`src/lib/logger.ts`): No synchronous file system operations at module load; pino transports handle directory creation

**Prisma Client** (`src/lib/db.ts`):
- Singleton pattern with `globalThis` caching in development only (prevents HMR connection leaks)
- In production (Vercel), each serverless function gets its own instance — no global caching needed

**Middleware** (`src/proxy.ts`, renamed from `middleware.ts` in Next 16.1):
- Matcher scoped to only dashboard routes (`/events/*`, `/dashboard/*`, `/settings/*`)
- Redirects REVIEWER and SUBMITTER from non-abstract event routes to `/events/[eventId]/abstracts`
- Public routes (`/e/*`), API routes (`/api/*`), auth pages, `/uploads/*`, and static assets skip middleware entirely

**Header Component** (`src/components/layout/header.tsx`):
- Uses React Query hooks (`useEvents`, `useEvent`) instead of manual `useEffect` fetching
- Data cached across navigation, preventing duplicate API calls

### React Query (Client-Side Caching)
Dashboard pages use React Query for client-side data caching. This provides:
- **Instant navigation:** Cached data displays immediately when returning to pages
- **Background refresh:** Data updates silently while showing cached content
- **Optimistic UI:** Mutations update cache immediately for responsive feel

**Configuration** (`src/components/providers.tsx`):
- `staleTime: 5 minutes` - Data considered fresh for 5 minutes
- `gcTime: 30 minutes` - Unused cache kept for 30 minutes
- `refetchOnWindowFocus: true` - Refresh when tab becomes active

**Using React Query hooks** (`src/hooks/use-api.ts`):
```typescript
// Fetching data (useTickets fetches registration types)
const { data: regTypes = [], isLoading, isFetching } = useTickets(eventId);

// Mutations with cache invalidation
const createRegType = useCreateTicket(eventId);
await createRegType.mutateAsync(formData);

// Manual cache invalidation
const queryClient = useQueryClient();
queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: queryKeys.tickets(eventId) });
```

**Available hooks:**
- `useTickets`, `useCreateTicket`, `useUpdateTicket`, `useDeleteTicket` (for registration types)
- `useRegistrations`, `useSpeakers`, `useImportRegistrationsToSpeakers`, `useSessions`, `useTracks`
- `useAbstracts`, `useHotels`, `useAccommodations`
- `useEventMedia`, `useUploadEventMedia`, `useDeleteEventMedia` (event-scoped media library)
- `useReviewers`, `useAddReviewer`, `useRemoveReviewer`
- `useEvents`, `useEvent`
- `useMedia`, `useUploadMedia`, `useDeleteMedia` (media library)
- `useSendCompletionEmails` (bulk send completion tokens to CSV-imported registrants)

## Recent Features

- **Student / member ID is a per-registration-type switch, not a guess at the type's NAME (September 2, 2026)** — Organizer ask: let them control whether the student ID and its expiry are required. The mechanism was a **name match** — a type whose name contained `member` asked for a membership number, one containing `student` asked for a student ID **and** its expiry — which is the identical anti-pattern the supporting-document feature retired on Aug 13, one field over. **Three new `TicketType` booleans** (`requiresMemberId` / `requiresStudentId` / `requiresStudentIdExpiry`) read through one client-safe [identity-evidence.ts](src/lib/identity-evidence.ts), shared by both public forms and both write routes so the form cannot ask for something the server ignores. **The live data is the argument.** `Resident` is the **most-registered type in this family — 6 registrations across 19 events — and matched neither pattern, so it asked for nothing at all**, which is not what any organizer who created a Resident rate meant; meanwhile `Trainee / Student` asked **only because of the slash in its name**. Renaming `Student` to `Undergraduate` silently switched verification off, with no warning and no log line. **Deliberately NO "ask but do not block" flag**, unlike the document switches: that distinction exists because a delegate may not have a PDF to hand at 11pm, whereas an ID number is something they know by heart, so asked means required and a second switch would be a control nobody sets. Expiry **nests under** the student ID in the UI, in the write route, and in the reader, because an expiry with nothing to expire is not a state an organizer can mean — resolved in the reader so no consumer has to remember it. **Migration `20260902120000` is additive + idempotent with a GATED backfill** (runs exactly once; a bare `WHERE requiresStudentId = false` would be re-runnable but would also re-enable a type an organizer had later switched off). Backfill is **exact parity, verified: zero disagreements with the old name match, and Resident deliberately stays silent** — turning verification on for 19 live events is a change nobody asked for, and the point is that the organizer can now do it themselves and see that they have. **Two pre-existing bugs closed on the way:** the completion form's requirement was **client-side only** — its route validated that a supplied expiry *parsed* but never that the fields were present, so the rule was one crafted request away from being skipped on a public token-gated link; and the registrant portal gated the student-ID row on the type's name, so a `Resident` registrant whose organizer had collected an ID could never see or edit it, the value existing while the row simply never rendered. **The clone drift-guard earned its keep**: it failed on the new columns and its own comment named the trap — under a name match a clone preserved the rule *for free* because the rule lived in the NAME, and a column does not, so a cloned "Student" rate would quietly stop verifying anyone. Clone route + guard updated together. `grep` now finds **no name-sniffing anywhere in `src/`**. +21 tests; the switch read and the expiry collapse are mutation-verified. **Not browser-verified:** the organizer dialog is unchecked in a browser — a second Next dev server refuses to start alongside the one this machine already has, and signing in on its port breaks the NextAuth callback.

- **Sponsors, their promo codes, and reporting what they brought, phase 1 (September 2, 2026)**: an organiser signs a sponsor, gives them a promo code, and wants to know at the end **who that sponsor brought**. Two populations arrive under one sponsor and **two different keys tracked them with nothing joining the two**: exhibitor staff by `Registration.sponsorId` + `INCLUSIVE`, invited doctors by the code they typed. **`PromoCode` had no sponsor column**, so a code belonged to its sponsor only by being named `ABBOTT20`, and the consequences were exactly what you would predict: the registrations list could not filter by sponsor, neither CSV export carried a Sponsor column although both carried Promo Code, and the promo page showed a redemption COUNT with no way to see who. **Two findings from reading the code reshaped the plan before any of it was built.** `sponsorId` was ALREADY accepted and validated on a paying registration and the UI hid the picker behind a single JSX condition, so the most-wanted half of the feature was **one condition away** the whole time; and sponsors live in `Event.settings.sponsors[]` with no FK and no delete guard, which the detail sheet already anticipates by rendering `(sponsor removed)`. **Shipped:** `PromoCode.sponsorId` (additive migration, **validated on write** rather than trusted, because adding a second unchecked pointer would have doubled the defect the feature exists to fix); the filter; a Sponsor column in both exports carrying the NAME resolved once per request, falling back to the id so a mis-wire is diagnosable rather than a blank that reads as "no sponsor"; the picker unhidden with its wording moved from payment to attribution; and the promo-codes GET now redacts, which it never did (it was already returning `discountValue` unredacted). **The filter unions THREE routes, and the third is the whole point.** A group registration puts the promo code on `RegistrationGroup.promoCodeId` and leaves every member's own `promoCodeId` null, so a two-arm query returns **zero** members of a twenty-person sponsor delegation, which is precisely the shape a delegation takes. It would have demoed correctly on one registration and under-reported the case it was built for. **An adversarial pass over the plan found six defects, three of which would have shipped** (that group arm, the FK semantics, the redaction), and is recorded in the plan's §9 rather than quietly fixed, because the failure mode generalises: **the current state was verified carefully and the proposed design was then not stressed against it.** `Restrict` was wrong twice over, since deleting an event cascades to Registration and Sponsor as siblings and SQL RESTRICT is checked immediately rather than deferred, and because the sub-theme precedent the plan itself cited is SetNull plus an application guard: **the draft quoted the right precedent and proposed the opposite mechanism.** **And ONE of the six findings was FALSE, which is worth as much as the five that were right.** It claimed sponsor attribution was inconsistent with the payer fields because MEMBER could see one and not the other. MEMBER has been in `FINANCE_ROLES` since the June-17 "desk staff record payments" decision, so neither is hidden from it; the claim came from the comment sitting directly above those keys in [finance-visibility.ts](src/lib/finance-visibility.ts), which still described the pre-June-17 rule. **In a codebase that records decisions in prose, a comment is evidence of what someone once decided, not of what the code now does. Read the predicate.** Both comments are corrected in place and a test pins the real boundary so the next reader cannot repeat it. The genuine question is left OPEN for the owner in ROADMAP: if MEMBER, ONSITE and WEBINARS must not learn who funds a doctor, `FINANCIAL_KEYS` is the wrong lever and it needs a narrower predicate the way the CRM's `canViewDealValues` is narrower than `canViewFinance`. **Deliberately incomplete, and stated exactly:** `PromoCode.sponsorId` is settable through **one** path, the promo-codes POST. Not the PUT, so **no EXISTING promo code can be attributed at all**; not MCP; and there is no picker on the Promo Codes page. The reporting half is fully live, the setting half is an API call. +12 tests (suite 6562 to 6574); phases 2 (sponsors as a table) and 3 (the per-sponsor rollup) recorded in ROADMAP.

- **A gate that counts the doors, and the HR screens finally run under RLS (September 2, 2026)** , Started as "I feel like we are missing something", and the missing thing was a category rather than a bug. **Every tenancy guard in the repo was a CONFORMANCE check, and conformance cannot see an absence.** [rls-apply.test.ts](__tests__/lib/rls-apply.test.ts) pins the properties of the policies that exist (FOR ALL not FOR SELECT, no NULL escape on reads, always a WITH CHECK, one GUC name, never FORCE); [check-tenant-als.sh](scripts/check-tenant-als.sh) pins that routes in a hand-listed set of directories take a lane, against a hand-maintained `SWEPT_MODELS` string; the other three police one rule each inside a known set. All of them answer *"is what we wrote correct"*. None answered *"did we write it at all"*, and **nothing in CI read `schema.prisma`**, so a model gaining `organizationId` and never getting a policy file was invisible. Not hypothetical: the Aug 21 audit found FOUR tables in exactly that state (`AbstractSubTheme`, `SpeakerProfileForm`, `AbstractSerialCounter`, `SessionProposalSerialCounter`), each with the column added AND the routes wrapped AND no policy. Two of three steps done correctly by people paying attention, and the third had nothing watching it; that audit was a manual pass and was never turned into a gate. New **[rls-coverage.test.ts](__tests__/lib/rls-coverage.test.ts)** is it: derives from the schema, and **resolves `@@map`**, which is the part that makes it non-trivial, since a policy targets the TABLE and `RsvpItem`/`RsvpResponse` are policied as `RsvpDinner`/`RsvpDinnerResponse` (renaming a live table is not blue/green safe). A naive model-name comparison reports those two as gaps forever, and a gate that cries wolf gets muted, which is worse than no gate. Three mutations verified: deleting a policy file names the model and prints the three steps to fix it, an allow-list entry for a table that IS policied fails, and dropping the `@@map` resolution fails in **both** directions at once (models look unpoliced AND policies look orphaned). The allow-list carries a reason per entry and three tests keep it honest (a stale entry for a deleted model fails, an entry for a policied table fails, a reason under 40 characters fails), so it can shrink by accident but cannot quietly grow. Today's tree: 92 models carry the column, 85 tables are policied, seven documented exceptions, most read *before* identity is resolved and therefore unprotectable by identity. **The second half is the same gap one layer up.** HR shipped Aug 27, **six days after** the Aug 21 sandbox rehearsal, and `setup-sandbox` had no HR fixtures, so six policied tables, twelve routes, seventeen lane wraps and fifteen harness assertions had never once been executed by the application under enforcement. That is the third instance of the identical shape (the operator lockout, the registrant portal, now HR), and it recurs structurally rather than through carelessness: **a rehearsal is a snapshot and the codebase keeps moving**, so anything built after one inherits none of its assurance. [seed-sandbox.ts](scripts/seed-sandbox.ts) now seeds the real leave-code catalogue (imported from `hr-seed-data.ts`, not retyped, so it cannot drift from what a live org gets), two employees, a month of attendance, an org-scoped standing rule and two holidays per tenant, with the **empCode and one holiday date colliding across orgs on purpose** so isolation is visible rather than merely asserted: each host must show its OWN row for the same key. `dev:sandbox` sets `HR_MODULE_ENABLED` and the tenant admin carries `User.hrAccess`, which exercises **both** arms of `canViewHr` (the flag and the role, since `super@sandbox.test` is sufficient by role alone). **Verified by hand on the running sandbox**, both hosts, then made repeatable: `npm run tenancy:isolation` gained two HR domains (13 to 15). AttendanceEntry is deliberately not one of them, and the reason is written down: its endpoint takes a date range against current-month fixtures, the harness already covers that policy with fifteen assertions, and the grid reads it through the employee lane the new row exercises. **Doc drift corrected in the same pass, all three previously flagged and none acted on:** PLATFORM_PROVISIONING called the identity model "still open" for twelve days after it shipped and warned about a NULL trap that `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` had already defused; PLATFORM_DECISIONS' status table said item 6 was DECIDED when it was BUILT, and its "what happens next" warned the registrant portal would return nothing on the platform, which the same day's work had fixed; SANDBOX.md said "only ~14 domains are swept" and listed five domains as unpolicied that all have policy files. Each is called out in place rather than quietly rewritten, because **a stale caution is worse than none**: it tells the reader an empty screen is expected, which is the exact symptom a real missing lane produces. +6 tests (suite 6549 to 6555); tsc, eslint, build clean.

- **The second HR workbook, and the sync that reads it without undoing anyone's work (August 31, 2026)** — The owner sent an updated `UAE_Employee_Attendance_Leave_Tracker_2026` the same afternoon the module went live, and the first thing the diff showed is that **the two sources had already diverged in both directions**: the workbook carried two carryovers (-10, +3), seven opening comp-offs, one future last working day and two removed leave days that prod did not have, while prod carried a carryover of 15, three leaver statuses and all 23 full names, typed into the app that morning, that the workbook did not. The import refuses a populated org by design, and applying the sheet blindly would have reverted a person's decisions, so the answer is a **`--sync`** mode on [import-hr-excel.ts](scripts/import-hr-excel.ts): a dry run that lists every difference, and a write that applies only what nobody in the app has overruled. **The rule is the app wins where a person edited it**, decided from evidence the system already keeps rather than from timestamps: an `Employee` audit row after the import marks a field as a decision (both audit shapes are read; a row the sync itself stamps `source: "import"` establishes nothing, or the third workbook could never move what the second set), and an attendance row whose `source` is not `import` is app-owned (re-coding an import row on the grid flips it to `ui`). Such fields and days are reported as conflicts and never touched; there is **no force flag**, deliberately, because the employee's page is where a person overrules a person. The reading of the sheet moved into a shared [hr-workbook.ts](scripts/hr-workbook.ts) and the planners into a pure [hr-sync-plan.ts](scripts/hr-sync-plan.ts), and every write goes through the same services the screens use, so the pair rule, the stranded-entries refusal, the range budget and the audit trail all apply and each row is attributed to `--actor`. **The gate itself had a bug the first workbook could not show.** Leave Summary D is entitlement PLUS carryover, and the gate read its entitlement from D and then added the engine's own carried-in figure: with every carryover at 0 it reconciled 22 of 23 and looked right; with -10 and +3 it flagged both as engine variances. It now reads Employee Master G, and a summary cell typed over its formula (Aimon's entitlement typed as 0 where the formula gives 30) is reported as the sheet disagreeing with itself and never as a reason to refuse. The status column is read the same way: a stale "Active" beside a past last working day yields RESIGNED, because the date is the fact and the word is a label time does not update. Applied to the local copy end to end (23 records, 5 days; a re-run converges to the one conflict), +17 tests, three guards mutation-verified. **Prod is the owner's to run** (the container needs the file, then the dry run, then the write), and the conflicts the dry run will list there are exactly the four people whose leaver status or carryover was decided in the app that morning: those stay as decided unless the owner changes them on the page. Two things the workbook says that only the owner can rule on and the sync deliberately does not touch: Aimon's entitlement typed as 0, and Adelina's entitlement typed as 30 the day before an anniversary she does not reach as a leaver.
- **HR module adversarial review, and batch 1 of its fixes (August 31, 2026)** — Three independent reviewer passes (security/tenancy/privacy · correctness/maths/concurrency · UI/drift/tests) plus a consolidating pass that re-verified every finding against source and reproduced the balance defects by running the engine: **0 BLOCKER / 6 HIGH / 14 MED / 13 LOW**, report at [docs/CODE_REVIEW_HR.html](docs/CODE_REVIEW_HR.html), deferred list in [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md) under "HR module review". The foundations held (narrow fail-closed predicate, API keys refused outright, every read and write org-bound, RLS + harness, audit rows stamped from the lane, no HR row reachable by a non-HR role through any surface). The defects were in three places. **(1) The balance engine failed open on two edges, both reachable from "Show leavers".** A year the person was not employed in turned `employedWindowInYear`'s `null` into `from = null, to = null`, and `isWithin` treats a null bound as OPEN, so a 2025 leaver's 2026 row summed their entire history against a fresh 30 (reproduced: entitlement 30, taken 5, balance 29); from 1 January 2027 that would have been every 2026 leaver. And the first-year gate was judged at today rather than at exit, so an eleven-month leaver flipped from 0 to 30 the day the calendar passed an anniversary they never reached, against the same-day ruling "zero unless first year is completed, leaver or not". Fixed: `computeLeaveBalance` returns `employedInYear: false` with zeros and the summary says so; the gate is judged at the earlier of today and the exit date. **The lesson is the shape, not the line: `null` meaning "open" in a helper and "nothing" in the caller's intent is the fail-open guard, and a balance "as at" a date has two clocks, the calendar and the employment.** **(2) Attendance history was unrecoverable after a mis-drag.** The grid's document-level key handler ignored modifiers, so with cells selected Cmd+C wrote comp-off, Cmd+A annual leave, Cmd+S sick leave and Cmd+W work-from-home as the tab closed (browsers do not honour `preventDefault` on Cmd+W); a held key auto-repeated the write. Clearing was an unbounded, unthrottled hard delete audited by count only, and an overwrite recorded the new code but not the old one and nulled the remark because the grid never sends remarks. Fixed: modifiers and repeat refused, `apply()` single-flight, the 366-day cap and the write rate bucket on DELETE, and both write and clear now snapshot the previous code of every affected day onto the audit row (codes only, never remarks), so a reversal can be done from the trail alone. **(3) Two recording paths price the same annual leave differently, and the docs disagreed with the code.** After `644bd60a` an explicit AL range charges every calendar day (weekends AND public holidays: the Eid week as AL costs 5), while a Company-day rule carrying AL charges working days only, because weekends and holidays are resolved before the rule; a two-week shutdown costs 12 from the grid and 10 as a rule, and both are pinned by tests that pass together. The service's own header, this file's "OPEN" paragraph and plan §6 all still described working-days-only. Owner ruling on the spot: **calendar days everywhere.** A rule whose code covers calendar days (`AttendanceRuleLike.category` + `rangeCoversCalendarDays`) now takes precedence over the holiday and the weekend, so an AL shutdown costs 12 as a rule and 12 from the grid, a public holiday inside an AL block is charged on both paths, and a WFH rule still stops at working days; the docs, the dialog copy and the user guide say so. **(4) The year-end roll existed only as a pure function (H6).** `LeaveGrant` was never read or written and `planYearRoll` had no caller, so every leave year used the go-live seeds; on the first working day of 2027 every 2026 overdraft or surplus would have vanished and the opening sick figure would have been charged again. Owner decision: the seed year lives on the row. New nullable `Employee.seedLeaveYear` (additive migration `20260831150000`, backfilled from `createdAt`; the workbook import writes 2026; `createEmployee` stamps the current year), and the engine applies `carryoverDays` and `openingSickUsed` in that year only, with a grant always winning. New [leave-year-roll-service.ts](src/hr/services/leave-year-roll-service.ts) writes one `LeaveGrant` per employee still employed on 1 January (carry-in from `planYearRoll`, capped in one direction; entitlement recorded but not read back, because the gate moves during the year; one audit row per run with the capped set), both balance paths read `carriedInDays` from the grant, and the **`hr-year-roll` worker job** (lease 1018, 01:05 UTC daily) runs it for every org **every night through January**, because the roll is an idempotent upsert that recomputes from the rows, so a December entry fixed on 5 January corrects the grant by itself. `POST /api/hr/leave-year/roll` and a "Re-run carry-over" button on the summary are the manual re-run for a correction made later. Six guards mutation-verified (each reverted line fails exactly its pinning test), +33 tests. **Process note:** two commits landed in the module while the review was running; the report was re-verified against the final tree rather than the one it started on. **M9 ruled the same afternoon** (owner: "the shutdown wins. Jinan is under AL or OFF as others, remaining days she is WFH"): a company-wide leave rule now outranks a person's standing WFH arrangement, so the permanently remote employee is on leave with everyone else during a shutdown and charged for it, is WFH the rest of the time, and her own recorded leave still overrides the arrangement (an explicit entry beats every rule). `ruleFor` decides time-not-worked over working (`isWorkingCategory`, WORK and ON_DUTY are the working categories) ahead of the EMPLOYEE-over-ORG order, and only when both rules carry a category, so a standing maternity rule still survives a company WFH week and an uncategorised rule is not guessed at. The "most recent decision wins" comment was corrected to what the code does (the later START date), and the two leftovers (overlaps not surfaced at create; start-date tiebreak) are LOWs in ROADMAP. Seven precedence tests plus a balance test, mutation-verified. **Batch 2 (owner: "ok go ahead", same afternoon) closed six MEDs.** *M2/M3/M6 in [employee-service.ts](src/hr/services/employee-service.ts)*: the status / last-working-day pair is judged on the RESULTING record by create and update alike (a leaver needs a date, an Active record cannot keep a past one, serving notice stays legal), a date move that would strand recorded attendance is refused with the count and range (`ENTRIES_OUTSIDE_WINDOW`; **no force flag, deliberately**, since the rows it would leave are exactly the ones the grid hides and the balance excludes), the write is `updateMany({ id, organizationId })` plus re-read with the harness pinning it as owner, and every default list decides "currently employed" from the last working day (`employedOnWhere`) rather than the status column, because **a status is a human record that time does not update**: before this the lists filtered on status while every window check read `exitDate`, so RESIGNED with no date was hidden everywhere and employed forever at once. *M1*: the grid fetches leavers and cuts rows to the people employed in the visible month. *M10*: one refetch per multi-person write, the selection kept on failure, "written for N of M, not written: who (why)". *M13*: the code popover is `position: fixed`, anchored to the head cell, re-placed on scroll, flips above a bottom row. +25 tests, the three service guards mutation-verified, prod copy checked read-only first (23 ACTIVE, no exit dates, zero stranded rows, so behaviour-preserving on live data). **Batch 3 (owner: "proceed to next batch") closed the remaining seven MEDs, so every MED in the report is now closed.** *M4*: a past year is "as at" its own 31 December and a year before the seed year with no grant is refused (`YEAR_NOT_HELD`). *M5*: a linked login must belong to the org, `userId: null` unlinks. *M7*: the employee audit is a field diff that records `notes` as changed and never quotes it (the attendance audit already refused remarks for the same reason: free text about a person will hold medical detail and the trail outlives the row); rule deletion now snapshots scope, code and dates. *M8*: holiday POST rate-limited and audited, a DELETE refused while attendance sits on the date, a **Holidays screen at `/hr/holidays`**, and 2027's fixed dates seeded while the Islamic ones stay HR-entered. *M11*: comp-off bounded by employment only, not by the clock. *M12*: range writes run under a 60 s transaction budget and a timeout is `WRITE_TIMED_OUT` (503) naming the size. *M14*: route-level tests for every HR route and a service-level test that a recorded day inside a rule window is charged once, the mutation the source-grep guard let through. +33 tests; five more guards mutation-verified. Deferred from M14: an e2e spec, since the e2e suite runs locally only.
- **HR module: attendance and UAE leave tracking, and the redesign that made recording bearable (August 27–31, 2026, owner-driven)** — Replaces the validated Excel tracker `UAE_Employee_Attendance_Leave_Tracker_2026 v5.1`, which stays the business-logic reference: where the plan and the workbook disagree, the workbook wins. Plan of record: [docs/HR_MODULE_PLAN.md](docs/HR_MODULE_PLAN.md). **Master silo only**, gated by `HR_MODULE_ENABLED` in [module-flags.ts](src/lib/module-flags.ts) — but the SCHEMA is tenant-correct from day one (`organizationId` on every table, RLS policies in `prisma/rls/`, harness assertions, CI-gate entries), because **a flag flips in a deploy and a tenant-blind data shape cannot**. Five tables (`Employee`, `LeaveCode`, `AttendanceEntry`, `LeaveGrant`, `PublicHoliday`), two enums, plus a confined **`HR_USER`** role. **The role sweep was the expensive part, not the enum value**: `RESTRICTED_WRITE_ROLES` is the ONE deny-list among the role predicates, so a role missing from it can write to every non-HR route, while every other predicate (finance / barcode / login / export / contacts) is an allow-list that excludes it for free.

  **Reading the workbook's FORMULAS rather than its numbers overturned two premises.** (1) The leave year is the **CALENDAR** year, not the service year — entitlement is a flat 30 gated on the first anniversary having passed, and the annual-leave `COUNTIFS` has no lower date bound — so the plan's original anniversary-lump model was wrong. (2) The workbook's comp-off formula is *"the previous day was also OD"*, but the owner's rule is *"both days of the SAME weekend"*; across 58 OD days on 16 employees **exactly one row diverges** (a Wed+Thu pair earning a comp-off that should not exist), so the import expects that single deliberate difference rather than treating it as a failure. Balance maths lives in ONE pure [leave-balance.ts](src/hr/lib/leave-balance.ts) — every surface calls it, there is deliberately no second implementation, because two of them disagree and the disagreement surfaces as a payroll figure. Calendar dates are `YYYY-MM-DD` **strings**, never `Date` objects (`getDay()` answers in the reader's timezone), and `@db.Date` appears here for the first time in the schema. Import reconciled **22 of 23 employees to the digit** against the workbook's own Leave Summary, with the one predicted comp-off variance; **prod holds 23 employees and 943 entries**.

  **Then the recording model was rebuilt, because the owner reported it as "a nightmare" — and the data said the form was not the problem.** Of the 386 work-from-home days imported, **252 are TWELVE company-wide dates** on which 20 to 22 people were all remote together (Ramadan, and the week after Eid), **120 belong to one permanently remote employee**, and **14 across five people are genuinely one-off**. So **386 rows were holding 27 facts**; March alone is 243 rows for 3 company days, 1 standing arrangement and 12 entries. The other 359 existed only because the schema had no way to say *"the company"* or *"always"*. New **`AttendanceRule`** (scope ORG or EMPLOYEE, a date range, a code, and the organiser's own words for why) **stores no days at all**: creating one writes nothing per person and removing one deletes nothing, because the days it covers were never rows — which is what makes a rule reversible and the hard delete safe. **Precedence lives in ONE place** ([hr-effective-status.ts](src/hr/lib/hr-effective-status.ts)): outside employment → explicit entry → public holiday → weekend → rule → assumed P, so a company day can never turn a Saturday into a working day; only an explicit OD does that. **The half that costs money**: a rule can carry any leave code, so a company-wide shutdown booked as AL has to reach payroll — **both** balance paths (one employee, and the org summary) expand rules through `ruleDerivedDays`, and because skipping it would hand everyone free annual leave with nothing on screen, the adoption is pinned at SOURCE level in both places and mutation-verified. The grid also became the input: drag across cells and press a key, with the five codes that are 99.3% of every entry carrying shortcuts. It now imports the shared resolver instead of the second copy of the precedence its own header had already worried about. **Deliberately NOT built:** a weekday filter ("every Friday") — individual non-company WFH is spread evenly across all five weekdays, so the data refuses it, and a contiguous range covers every real case in the file.

  **One bug found by a user, worth keeping for its shape.** Setting a code from the popover's "Another code…" dropdown silently did nothing — and not for one code: **16 of the 21 were unreachable**, because they all live behind it. Radix renders a `Select`'s list in a **PORTAL**, so an option is not a DOM descendant of the popover; the popover's click-away handler read the click as "outside", unmounted itself, and took the Select with it before `onValueChange` could fire. Verified in a browser: popover closed, no toast, no error, **zero network requests**, cell unchanged — nothing reached `/logs` because nothing failed, the code never ran. **Generalise it: a portal breaks every "is this click inside me?" check**, and the debugging shortcut is that *zero* requests distinguishes "the handler never ran" from "it ran and failed" in one glance. Fixed by removing the class rather than patching against a Radix internal — the secondary codes are an inline grid inside the popover's own subtree — and the regression guard is structural (that popover may contain no `Select`, `Popover`, `Dialog`, `DropdownMenu`, `Tooltip` or `createPortal`), mutation-verified.

  **RULED, Aug 31 2026 (`644bd60a`): the weekend annual-leave fork.** 86 of 419 imported AL days sit on a Saturday or Sunday, plus 4 on public holidays, because the workbook charged a holiday block in **calendar** days. The owner ruled that the app must match the workbook: an explicit annual-leave range now charges every calendar day in the block (`rangeCoversCalendarDays` in [hr-constants.ts](src/hr/lib/hr-constants.ts)), so a two-week holiday costs 12 whether it was imported or recorded today; sick leave stays working-days-only because the data showed the workbook recorded it that way. **Closed the same day (review H3, [docs/CODE_REVIEW_HR.html](docs/CODE_REVIEW_HR.html)):** a Company-day RULE carrying AL used to charge working days only, because weekends and public holidays were resolved before the rule, so the same shutdown cost 10 as a rule and 12 from the grid. Owner ruling: **calendar days everywhere.** A rule whose code covers calendar days now beats the holiday and the weekend in [hr-effective-status.ts](src/hr/lib/hr-effective-status.ts) (a working-day rule such as WFH still cannot make a Saturday a working day), so an AL shutdown costs the same whichever way it was recorded, and a public holiday inside an AL block is charged on both paths. **Also still open:** an HR settings screen for leave codes (the holidays screen shipped Aug 31), dashboard tiles, MCP tools, and the privacy paragraph in [SECURITY_AND_PRIVACY_POSTURE.md](docs/SECURITY_AND_PRIVACY_POSTURE.md) — that database now holds colleagues' sick-leave records while the document handed to EHS describes it as event data.

- **A Codex PR reviewed and merged as a subset (August 31, 2026 — PR #33)** — Three tools proposed; one taken as written, one rewritten, one dropped. **Taken:** nine `.catch(() => {})` cleanup handlers became logged warnings. That shape is how an incident hides — the call fails, the request still returns 200, nothing reaches `/logs` — and all nine were best-effort deletions of expired verification tokens and spent OAuth codes, so a database incident could leave live public tokens accumulating with no trace. **Rewritten:** the gate that keeps them fixed ([check-no-silent-server-catches.sh](scripts/check-no-silent-server-catches.sh)) used `mapfile` and `rg`; macOS ships bash 3.2 (no `mapfile`) and BSD grep (no `\s`), so it died at exit 127 on every developer machine here while all four existing gates run fine — **a CI check you can only reproduce by pushing is one you debug by pushing**. Its allow-list now carries a reason PER ENTRY, because the original's single blanket justification ("browser media playback") was true of one entry and false of the other, which is a keepalive `fetch` beacon. The **logger** change is kept but **latched**: stderr rather than pino is right (that code IS a pino stream, so logging through it would recurse into the sink that just failed), but unlatched it printed every 2 seconds for the length of an outage — it now reports once and re-arms on the next success. `preflight-dev.mjs` is scoped per command; it asserted `vitest`/`eslint`/`typescript` for `build`, which runs inside the production image, coupling it to devDependencies it never invokes. **Dropped: the RLS status doc and script**, for three reasons each verified by running them — the checklist marked **9 of 10 domains PENDING** when the Phase-2 sweep queue has been EMPTY since Aug 4 and `prisma/rls/` holds 47 policy files; the script **exits 1 with no output at all the moment every domain is COMPLETE** (`rg -c` exits 1 on no match, `set -e` kills the assignment) while wired in as a *gating* step, so CI would go red on every push on the day the work finished; and `--require-ready` demanded zero files matching `db.$transaction(`, which includes [db.ts](src/lib/db.ts) where `tenantTransaction` is defined by wrapping it, plus five `api/auth/*` identity routes that are deliberately cross-org. **The reusable lesson: both new tools failed in the same direction — they looked fine until a future date.** One passed CI while being unrunnable locally; the other passed CI while wired to break on success. Neither is visible in a green checkmark, which is why running a tool in its SUCCESS state is worth the thirty seconds.

- **An id in a log line now resolves to a name (August 27, 2026, owner request)** — Log lines name rows by id and nothing else, so `{"eventId":"cmt8fkgbl…"}` said which row was involved and nothing about which event it was; answering that meant a psql session, and `prod:psql` is read-only-by-courtesy, so the cheapest possible question had the most expensive available answer. New **[/admin/lookup](src/app/(dashboard)/admin/lookup/page.tsx)** takes an id and gives back the name, plus the parent event and organisation. **It resolves EVERY id-bearing model rather than taking a type**, because the log line labels the id only sometimes — a bare id in a Prisma P2025 message carries no key at all — so asking the operator to know the type would fail precisely where the tool is most needed. That costs nothing: one `findMany … id IN (…)` per model means the price is fixed by the number of MODELS, not by how many ids were pasted, which is also what makes the box accept **a whole pasted log line** and resolve every id in it at once. Model coverage was picked from evidence rather than intuition — grepping the id keys that actually appear inside `apiLogger` calls ranks them eventId 409, userId 318, registrationId 79, organizationId 50, speakerId 46 — and 22 models are covered, each one entry in a plain array so adding the next is six lines. **Both walls** (multi-tenancy item 5): `denyNonOperator` for RBAC and `dbOperator` for the lane, because an id in a log line may belong to any tenant and a single lane would return zero rows for exactly the ids an operator needs to identify; the route is added to `OPERATOR_LANE_ALLOWLIST` in [check-tenant-als.sh](scripts/check-tenant-als.sh), which is a security decision and not a build fix. Every statement is a `findMany`, so it is read-only by construction. **The other half is on /logs itself**: every cuid in a rendered line is now a link into the lookup, since the question arises *there* and an answer that needs a copy-paste into another screen is one the operator will not bother asking. **The extraction rules are the part worth testing** and they live in a pure [id-lookup.ts](src/lib/id-lookup.ts) so the test needs no database: a paste with cuids yields those, a lone opaque token is tried as-is (a Stripe `pi_…`, an invoice number — a clean miss beats refusing to look), and **prose or compact JSON with no id in it yields NOTHING**. That last guard is the one that matters, and writing the test is what found the hole: the first cut accepted any whitespace-free string, and `{"msg":"worker:tick-end"}` has no whitespace either, so a JSON line with no ids in it would have gone into a database query as one "id". The rule is now an opaque-token shape, not merely an absence of spaces. Verified in a browser both ways — an ADMIN gets the refusal card and no sidebar entry, a SUPER_ADMIN resolves a real event and a real registration with event + org names, and on /logs exactly 3 of 100 rendered lines carry a link, matching the 3 that contain an id. +9 tests (suite 6243).

- **The door admits only PAID, COMPLIMENTARY and INCLUSIVE + three kiosk fixes (August 27, 2026, owner)** — **(1) Check-in gate tightened**, reversing the July 11 ruling that a failed charge or a goodwill refund should not bar someone from the venue, and additionally excluding **UNASSIGNED** — the default for an admin-created registration whose payment is still pending, which the old rule admitted **only by omission**. **The tightening initially did nothing for the commonest case, and finding out why is the useful part.** An UNPAID attendee owing 100 turned up checked in *after* the change: `isComplimentaryRegistration` short-circuits ahead of the allow-list, and it read `ticketTypePrice === 0 || pricingTierPrice === 0` — but the standard shape here is a **base ticket type priced 0 with the real money on the tier** (Early Bird, Standard), so "Physician 0.00 + Standard 100.00" read as FREE and was admitted regardless of payment status. **`registration-financials.ts` had solved exactly this in July** for the money screens — its own comment reads *"the row reads as a 'Free registration' while it actually owes the tier price"* — so the door was carrying a second, wrong copy of a rule that was already right elsewhere. Fixed by **calling the correct one** (`readRegistrationBasePrice`) rather than repairing the duplicate, so the door and the invoice can no longer disagree about what someone owes; `originalPrice` is now selected and passed at all four call sites. **This blocks 11 unpaid tier-priced registrations across four live events** who previously walked in free, which is precisely what the request asked for. **REFUNDED is the one exception and it turns on the REGISTRATION status, not the money** (same-day refinement): a refund and a cancellation are different facts, so money going back while the registration stays CONFIRMED is the organiser saying the place still stands (a sponsor picked up the cost, or goodwill), while someone genuinely not coming gets CANCELLED — which the gate refuses a branch earlier. **FAILED gets no such exemption**, because there the money never arrived at all and CONFIRMED only means nobody has chased them yet. The live case: HEMNET 2026 holds exactly one CONFIRMED+REFUNDED registration, **already through the door**, whom the first cut would have refused on a re-scan. `status` was made a **REQUIRED** field on the predicate rather than optional, so the compiler named every caller — the badge route was not passing it, and an optional field would have silently admitted at the door while printing no badge, which is the exact H1 drift the shared predicate exists to prevent. Otherwise `isPaymentAdmissible` is an **ALLOW-list**, and that shape is the point: a status added to the `PaymentStatus` enum later is refused until somebody decides otherwise, rather than admitted because nobody remembered to add it to a deny-list — which is exactly how UNASSIGNED/FAILED/REFUNDED came to be admitted in the first place. Checked read-only before shipping: across **every upcoming event this newly blocks TWO registrations** (one REFUNDED, one UNASSIGNED on a test event), so the blast radius is nil. **Badge printing follows in step, deliberately** — the badge route derives from the same predicate so a badge is printed for exactly the people the door will admit and nobody is handed one that will not let them in. **The desk override (`allowPaymentDue`) is untouched**, so this narrows the DEFAULT, not the desk's authority; pinned by a test asserting all five refused statuses still pass with the override. **(2) Kiosk "already checked in" clears in 2s** instead of 10 — it is the most common rescan at a busy door, needs no reading and no action, and holding the screen puts the next person in a queue behind a message saying nothing is wrong. The reprint-cap refusal keeps the long timeout (it needs reading) and a successful reprint keeps 8s (a badge is physically printing). **(3) Esc opens the staff PIN pad**, sharing one code path with the 5-tap corner gesture. **It opens the pad; it does not leave** — Esc-as-exit would undo the reason the PIN exists (review H1), and the kiosk has a keyboard attached *by design* since the barcode scanner is a keyboard wedge, so anything a bare key can do the hardware in the attendee's hand can do too. **(4) The kiosk wears the EVENT's branding**, not the organisation's: it stands in the lobby *of an event*. A **chain** (`emailHeaderImage → bannerImage → org logo`, footer from `emailFooterImage`) rather than one field, because events are configured unevenly — verified read-only that of 12 upcoming events 7 have a banner, 5 an email footer and only 2 an email header, **including the one being rehearsed with, which has a banner and nothing else**, so picking a single field would have shown nothing on the very screen this was asked for. The header chip is sized to hold a wide banner as well as a square logo; the footer is `pointer-events-none` so it cannot swallow a tap meant for the corner exit target at the same edge. **Also fixed:** a **flaky assertion I shipped this morning** in the local-DB guard suite — snapshot filenames are stamped per SECOND, so under load two can share a stamp and `ls -1t` orders them arbitrarily; it failed once in four full runs. Now asserts the OLDEST was pruned (three seconds clear of any tie) rather than that a specific newest survived, which is the property that actually matters. +2 tests, 2 repinned (suite 6230); the allow-list is mutation-verified.

- **DTCM codes can be shared between two registrations (August 27, 2026, owner decision)** — The desk hit `Unique constraint failed on the fields: (dtcmBarcode)` twice during the Aug-28 badge rehearsal, 19 minutes apart, trying to put one compliance code on a second person. Owner ruling, asked and reaffirmed after the trade-off was put in writing: **two people may share a code.** Migration `20260827060000` drops the global `@unique`; a plain index replaces it, since that column is read on every check-in scan. **Only LOOSENS, so it is blue/green safe** — every write the old container makes keeps working and simply stops colliding (same shape as the RSVP `20260814120000` drop); verified read-only first that prod held 10 codes, all live, **zero duplicates**, so no existing row changes meaning. **The consequences are handled rather than pretended away, and they are not the ones the original design feared.** The pool's spare maths is **unaffected** — `spare` derives from a Set of held codes, so it counts DISTINCT codes and a shared one still counts once. What actually breaks is **identification**: check-in accepts either the entry barcode or the DTCM code, and a shared code matches two rows, where the previous `findFirst` would have checked in whichever one Postgres returned and left the other un-checked-in with nothing saying why. The scan route now **refuses an ambiguous DTCM match** (409 `AMBIGUOUS_SCAN`) naming the entry barcode as the way out; an entry-barcode match always wins and is never ambiguous, so **the ordinary desk flow is untouched**. Second break: the pool used the constraint AS its contention signal (a second station's claim got P2002 and moved on), so `claimSpareDtcmCode` now re-reads the holders after claiming and keeps the code only if it is the lowest registration id among them, else releases and takes the next spare — **deterministic on purpose, because both racers backing off would leave a walk-up with no code at all**, the exact outcome the pool exists to prevent. Note the asymmetry, which is the design: **a HUMAN typing a code may duplicate it; the POOL never does**, or "N spare" on the desk strip stops meaning anything. Sharing is now **logged** (`registration-update:dtcm-code-shared`, both ids, truncated code) because the constraint used to be the only thing that noticed — the per-row audit shows a row GAINING a code, never that someone else already had it. **Two things stated rather than hidden:** re-adding the constraint is only possible while the data is duplicate-free, which it will not be once the desk uses this; and nothing now prevents one credential covering two people at a DTCM-inspected door, which was previously impossible and is now a policy question. New [docs/DTCM.md](docs/DTCM.md) is the reference (three writers, why availability is derived and never stored, who may see a code, the known gaps). **Also fixed in passing:** the alert that surfaced this was a false page — Prisma's connector fires its own error-level event BEFORE application code catches the exception, so a cleanly-handled collision (the service already logged `registration-update:unique-constraint` at warn and returned a 4xx) still sent an admin email. +6 tests (suite 6225); the ambiguity refusal and the pool tie-break are both mutation-verified.

- **Event variables are global, and the email that proved why (August 27, 2026)** — Owner rule: `eventName` / `eventDate` / `eventVenue` must resolve in **every** email template, not be opted into per slug. They were not, and the failure is nastier than a blank: `renderTemplate` deliberately leaves an unknown token **in place**, so a template using a token its particular sender happened not to build rendered the **literal `{{eventDate}}`** in the delivered email. **The organizer could not have caught it, because the PREVIEW supplies event variables for every slug** — it rendered correctly on screen and wrongly in the inbox. Same preview/send divergence class as the Aug 12 `{{eventDateRange}}` bug, and it shipped: **Middle East Heart Failure 2027 (PUBLISHED, 4 abstracts) mailed real authors *"which will be held from `{{eventDate}}` at `{{eventVenue}}`"*, braces and all.** **The fix rides on `branding`** ([email.ts](src/lib/email.ts) `EmailBranding.eventVars`), because branding is the one object every sender already threads from `getEventTemplate` into `renderAndWrap` — so it reaches every slug with **no per-caller wiring**, which is the part that stops the next hand-built sender reproducing it. The fields join the event `select` `getEventTemplate` **already runs**, so it costs no extra query, and dates go through the existing `buildEventDateTokens` rather than a fresh `Intl` call (it anchors to the event's timezone, and formatting an event date without one silently moves the **date**, not just the clock). **Precedence is the load-bearing part and is mutation-verified:** signature default < global event block < caller, so a sender that already builds its own `eventDate` keeps winning and nothing that was correct changes. **Scope, measured rather than assumed:** a first pass said 209 of 577 active templates use an undeclared token — that number is **documentation drift, not breakage**, because `TEMPLATE_VARIABLES` is a doc list while senders pass whatever they like. Chased down, exactly **one** slug was genuinely broken (`abstract-submission-confirmation`); every other slug using event tokens has a sender that supplies them (`bulk-email` covers speaker-invitation/agreement, registration-confirmation, payment-reminder, event-reminder; plus payment-confirmation, group-registration, certificates), and `refund-confirmation` is a **dead template** that 20 events still keep a copy of but nothing has sent since partial refunds landed in July. **Also closed a second, pre-existing divergence found on the way:** `buildEventPreviewVariables` formatted its own dates short ("Fri, Jan 15, 2027") while the send formats long, under a comment asserting the two matched. Both now derive from the one helper, so agreement is structural instead of a claim. Two existing assertions pinned the old divergence (`eventDateRange === eventDate` as *strings*, which the send has never done) and were replaced with the real contract — same day, different format — which is stronger than the equality they had. **The template drift underneath all this is the durable lesson:** `DEFAULT_TEMPLATES` is a **seed**, not a live default. The templates list materialises a per-event row on first view, so **26 events hold a frozen copy** of the abstract confirmation and editing the default in code reaches **one** of them. `{{abstractNumber}}` (Aug 4) and `{{travelGrantBlock}}` (Aug 25) were in **no** live copy, which means switching Travel Grant on would have skipped every overseas author **silently**. New [scripts/repair-abstract-confirmation-templates.ts](scripts/repair-abstract-confirmation-templates.ts) repairs the events that actually have abstracts: dry-run by default, idempotent, and **anchor-based — a missing anchor is reported and skipped rather than guessed at**, because these are organizers' own hand-edited templates and their prose is theirs. It also repairs MEHF's table, where somebody had duplicated the "Status: Submitted" row and renamed the labels without changing the values, so authors were told *Paper Number: Submitted / Theme: Submitted / Presenting Author: (blank)* with the real co-author names orphaned outside the styled body. +6 tests, precedence mutation-verified both directions.

- **Tab walked out of the check-in kiosk into the staff dashboard (August 26, 2026)** — Found while verifying that the kiosk's new branding renders, which is the point worth keeping: the branding was fine, and looking at it in a browser surfaced something a test never would. The kiosk page renders **inside the `(dashboard)` route group**, so the sidebar stays mounted in the DOM behind the full-screen overlay: invisible, but its links are still focusable. Fifteen Tab presses from the scan screen put focus on `/dashboard` and `/events/{id}/registrations`, and Enter follows the link — the full delegate list with payment status and entry barcodes, in front of whoever is standing at the machine. **It bypasses the exit PIN rather than defeating it**: the PIN guards the on-screen five-tap corner gesture and this route never goes near it. The existing 1-second focus reclaim pulls focus back, which is far longer than Tab-then-Enter takes. **What makes it live rather than theoretical is that the kiosk has a keyboard attached BY DESIGN** — the barcode scanner is a keyboard wedge, so the hardware needed to do it is already plugged in and pointed at the attendee. Fixed with a capture-phase keydown listener beside the focus guards already in that file, delegating to a pure `shouldTrapKioskTab` in [kiosk-focus.ts](src/lib/kiosk-focus.ts); the staff PIN pad is deliberately exempt (a real form that needs Tab, and the one surface where staff have already proven control by knowing the gesture). Extracted rather than left inline **because the regression is silent** — reopen the hole and the kiosk looks and behaves identically, only the reachable surface changes. Verified in a browser both ways (15 Tabs never leave the input, the scanner still receives keystrokes afterwards, Tab moves freely once the pad opens) and the predicate is mutation-verified in both directions. The structurally cleaner fix — moving the kiosk out of the dashboard route group so no shell exists — was **rejected**: the launch URL is baked into `chrome --kiosk` shortcuts on real machines and printed in the user guide, so changing it would break every kiosk already set up.

- **Travel grants: the organizer picks which countries count as local (August 26, 2026)** — The exempt country was hard-coded to the UAE, which is one customer's geography baked into a shared feature: a Riyadh conference would have offered grants to its own locals and withheld them from everyone in Dubai. It is now `settings.travelGrant.homeCountries`, an ISO alpha-2 list picked in Settings → Abstracts. **The change made the module smaller** — a special case became the general case, rather than a second special case being added beside the first. **Everything resolves to a CODE before comparing**, because `Speaker.country` holds a display name from `CountrySelect`, legacy rows hold `"AE"`, and the CSV importers write free text: a name comparison would class a code-holding row as overseas and mail a grant offer to a local resident. A short alias table covers what people actually type (`uae`/`uk`/`usa`/`ksa`, plus the UAE's alpha-3 `are` which was recognised before); every entry only converts a previously-FLAGGED row into a correctly-routed one, and alpha-3 is deliberately not general because `countries.ts` carries no alpha-3 column. **`unknown` still never means eligible** and the reason got stronger, not weaker: `"Dubai"` was always a reachable free-text value in the UAE, and the trap multiplies once the home country is configurable (`"Riyadh"`, `"Doha"`) — enumerating cities fails OPEN on the ones you forget, falling through fails CLOSED. **The one place the intuitive reading fails open is "switched on, no country named"**: an empty exempt set classifies every recognised country as overseas, so the feature would offer a grant to every local author — `readTravelGrantSettings` therefore reports it as **disabled**, and returns a separate `misconfigured` flag so the settings card can say why rather than looking merely off. The classifier fails closed the same way even if reached directly. **The label became a function** (`residencyLabel`): one home country names itself ("United Arab Emirates, not eligible"), two or more shorten to "Local, not eligible" with the full list in the settings card, the console tile's hover and the badge's `title` (owner decision) — and the exhaustive `switch` catches a fourth residency class at COMPILE time, which the `Object.keys` test it replaced could only catch at runtime. Migration `20260826120000` backfills `homeCountries: ["AE"]` onto any event already switched on, so this is behaviour-preserving rather than merely harmless; on prod that was exactly one row (a test event, zero grant rows). **Save is deliberately NOT blocked** when the switch is on with no country — one Save covers the whole tab, so blocking would stop unrelated settings saving (the M9 class); the reader fails closed and an amber panel explains it. **Two things the browser check caught that four green gates did not**: the console page read `data.homeCountries.length` off a response type, which is `undefined.length` and a white page when a new bundle meets an old container (now coerced once at the render entry, the way the speaker card already did); and the tab's only Save button sat at the foot of the *Submissions* card with Travel Grant below it, so the button that persists the new required field was scrolled off above it — moved below the card it saves. **Two review findings decided in-band:** a half-edited country list no longer kills outstanding consent links (the public route gates on `switchedOn` — did the organizer switch it OFF — rather than `enabled` — is it usable; residency is decided when a grant is MINTED, and answering the form does not depend on the exempt list, so emptying the list to change it would have shown the author the same "invalid or already used" message as a forged token); and "remind everyone pending" now re-checks residency against the CURRENT countries, which the named-send path already did — **two resolvers in one function disagreeing about who is eligible was the actual defect**, and skipped authors are counted and logged while keeping a live link, because withdrawing an offer already made is a human decision the console surfaces. +45 tests (suite 6183); five mutations verified (an empty exempt set falling through to `overseas`, `enabled: true` standing without a country, and resolving by display name only each fail exactly the right cases).

- **Spare DTCM codes for walk-ups — a pool the desk draws from, and the badge round that preceded it (August 25–26, 2026)** — DTCM issues a **block** of compliance codes a day or two before a Dubai event. The pre-event CSV maps most of them onto people who have already registered; **the leftovers had nowhere to live**, because `Registration.dtcmBarcode` needs a registration to hang on, so someone registering at the counter on the morning got no code and their badge printed with no compliance QR. New `DtcmCode` table (additive migration `20260825140000`, `@@unique([eventId, code])`, born tenancy-compliant — org stamped at write, `runWithTenantLane`, [prisma/rls/dtcmcode.sql](prisma/rls/dtcmcode.sql), a 9-assertion harness test where both orgs hold the SAME code, and a `check-tenant-als.sh` entry). **The one design decision worth carrying:** availability is **derived, never stored** — a code is spare iff no registration on that event holds it, and there is deliberately no `assignedRegistrationId` column. The stored flag is tempting (one indexed query instead of two) and wrong here, because **three independent writers already touch `Registration.dtcmBarcode`** (the CSV importer, the detail sheet's free-text field, this module) and a flag would have to be reconciled by every one of them; miss one and the pool believes a code is spare while an attendee is wearing it, which hands the same compliance credential to two people. Concurrency uses **the constraint that already exists** rather than a lock: `dtcmBarcode` is globally unique, so a second station's write fails P2002 and we take the next spare — no advisory lock, no transaction held across a desk interaction, and correctness does not depend on which connection ran what (the June-2026 pooler lesson). `claimSpareDtcmCode` **never throws**: a walk-up whose registration committed must not be rolled back because a compliance block ran out. **Claimed automatically on every create path** (registration-service → REST + MCP, and the public register route), **awaited not fire-and-forget**, because the desk prints a badge seconds later and a code arriving after the print is a badge with no QR on it. **The intake was the part that had to be got right.** The import route required a `registrationId` or `email` column and 400'd without one — correct for a file of assignments, and it made the pool **unfillable**, so the feature shipped Aug 25 and was **inert until Aug 26**. Dropping the guard would have opened a worse hole: a file whose owner column is called `attendee_email` looks *identical* to a file with no owner column, so inferring "these are spares" there turns 200 intended assignments into 200 unclaimed codes while reporting success. So the mode is **DECLARED** in the import dialog (Assign to people / Spare codes for the desk), never sniffed — the rule the Freshsales importer settled on for date order, that a guess which is usually right is exactly the failure mode. The mode relaxes only the *column* requirement: a row naming someone is still assigned in either mode, and a row naming an owner we **cannot resolve** stays an ERROR rather than quietly becoming a spare, because the person it was meant for would otherwise arrive with none and nothing would have said so. The assign-mode refusal names the columns it found and points at the other mode, so it is self-service rather than a dead end. **Surfaced where it is consumed:** a strip above the registrations list (amber at 10 spares, red at 0) because "0 spare" is invisible otherwise — the registration succeeds, the badge just prints without a QR, and the gap is found by an inspector rather than by us; a **walk-up warning** on both create surfaces from ONE shared `dtcmWalkupWarning` helper (silent for virtual attendees, who get no badge, and silent when the flag has not loaded — a spurious warning on every ordinary registration trains the desk to dismiss the real one); and **Assign a spare code** on the registration detail sheet. **Security fix found in review (B1):** the pool route was gated on `REGISTRATION_DESK_ALLOW` alone, which is the right answer to *who staffs the desk* and the wrong answer to *who may hold a door credential* — that allow-list includes MEMBER, `BARCODE_ROLES` deliberately excludes it. Not write-only: the `already-has-code` outcome is a pure READ of the code on someone else's row, and because MEMBER's registration payloads are **redacted**, every row rendered "Not set" so the button was offered on all of them — **redaction made the leak worse, turning it into one click per registration across every event in the org**. Both verbs now compose the two predicates, refusing before the rate-limit budget is spent. **Shipped alongside** (organizer-reported, same round): the custom badge type was saving correctly but the sheet's Select could not display it (a display bug diagnosed by probing the DB before reading code) — now derived by one pure `resolveBadgeTypeField`; a **barcode/QR arrangement** setting (stacked, both centred, or side-by-side — which costs the entry barcode ~17mm, taking a 4″ badge from ~80mm to ~64mm and still clearing the ~60mm scanners want, with a save-time warning when it does not); the registration number moved under the name; the Undo Check-in button fixed (shadcn's `outline` variant sets `bg-background` but **no text colour**, so it inherited white-on-white from the gradient header); and **kiosk badge reprint is now opt-in, off by default** so an attendee prints once. +36 tests across the arc (17 pool unit, 18 route RBAC, 12 import-mode, 7 walk-up, plus badge-layout cases); the assign-mode guard, the safe default, the MEMBER refusal and the virtual exemption are each **mutation-verified**. **Not yet built** (ROADMAP §"DTCM spare pool"): group-registration / MCP-bulk / speaker-companion creates skip the claim; only the first 10 spares are tried and every caller starts at `spares[0]`; the availability read is two full-table scans on the public register hot path; a cancelled registration holds its code forever.

- **Session expiry stops rendering an empty page, and mobile finally honours revocation (August 25, 2026)** — Two findings from reading 22 hours of production warnings, plus adopting a rule off the back of them. **(1) The reported symptom:** four `crm-route:unauthorized` warnings, part of 26 over two weeks in three bursts — **fifteen CRM routes 401'ing inside ninety seconds**, then the same contact record retried three minutes later. That shape is a person, not a scanner: a scanner probes random URLs, it does not come back after three minutes to retry one particular contact. Their 48h session had expired under an open tab, every React Query hook refetched, and the page rendered **empty lists** with no sign-in prompt. A page LOAD was never affected (the dashboard layout server-redirects), so only the already-open tab broke. **The load-bearing part of the fix is not the new file.** The app has three fetchers with three error shapes, and `fetchApi` — which backs the entire core dashboard — threw a bare `Error` with **no status at all**, so a handler keyed on `ApiError` would have fixed the CRM and silently missed everything else; it now throws `ApiError` with the message unchanged, so every existing catch is untouched. The redirect lives in `QueryCache.onError` (the one place every client query AND mutation failure lands) and **deliberately refuses the check-in kiosk** — attendee-facing, full-screen, PIN-gated exit, so bouncing it would put a staff password box in front of a queue of delegates; it keeps its own red state. Public `/e/{slug}/*` pages go to their own branded login. 401/403 are no longer retried, and the Sentry 4xx skip reads the real status instead of regex-matching the message for a three-digit number. **(2) The finding nobody reported:** chasing "what happens if a JWT is stolen" found that `deactivatedAt` closed the web door and **not the mobile one**. `mobile-login` had no deactivation check at all, so a deactivated account could sign in and collect a fresh 24h access token plus a **30-day refresh token**; `mobile-refresh` re-read the user but asked only whether they still *existed*, so a stolen refresh token kept minting access tokens for its full life and only *deleting* the account stopped it. **So "deactivate the account" was a complete answer on web and a false one on mobile — the worst kind of control, one an operator reasonably believes they have used.** Both doors now route through the existing `decideSessionValidity` rather than a parallel check, the payload carries `tokenVersion` stamped from the **row** (not laundered forward from the presented token), and the deactivation refusal sits after the password compare so there is no account-state oracle. Verified before shipping: prod has **0 mobile logins ever, 0 device tokens, and all 129 users at `tokenVersion` 0**, so it is preventative and changed nothing for anyone. The access path stays signature-only by choice, its 24h ceiling marked with a `ponytail:` comment naming both upgrade paths — a per-request DB lookup to shorten a bounded window is the wrong trade, and what makes it bounded is that both doors which could *extend* it now check. **(3) Adopted [Ponytail](https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail)'s laziness ladder as AGENTS.md rule 10**, amended. Not as the answer to the Aug 24 bugs — all three were minimal, correct code that failed in relation to something outside its file, and a rule that makes you write less would not have caught any of them. Adopted because the over-building problem is separately evidenced here: a **449-line** certificate resend route with zero callers, `storedFileExists` imported by nothing, two notification switches **read by nothing for months** while an event with both `false` kept sending. Two additions to their "not lazy about" list, because theirs omits both: **every failure path still logs** (rule 2 outranks a shorter diff), and **the comment recording why a guard exists** (their `ponytail:` marker names a ceiling; ours also names the incident). First application was to my own work: a seven-entry guard list in `session-expiry.ts` where **six entries defended paths that cannot produce the error at all**, trimmed the same day, 52 code lines down to 41. **Also corrected:** CLAUDE.md still claimed "nothing can sign anyone out", which `tokenVersion` superseded on Aug 11. **Known and deliberately not built:** `hashVerificationToken` peppers with `NEXTAUTH_SECRET` and those hashes are **stored**, so rotating the secret irreversibly invalidates every outstanding reset / verification / invitation / survey / RSVP / agreement link — `NEXTAUTH_SECRET_FALLBACK` covers credential decryption only. Sized at ~13 call sites for a once-ever break-glass action whose consequence is "everyone needs a new link", so it is documented in ROADMAP rather than built. +30 tests across the two changes (21 session-expiry, 9 mobile revocation); **nine guards mutation-verified** — removing the kiosk carve-out, reverting `fetchApi` to a bare Error, latching on a declined redirect, reverting the retry policy, dropping the mutationCache wiring, removing the mobile deactivation gate, reverting `mobile-refresh` to an existence check, laundering a stale counter forward, and un-stamping the mint sites each fail exactly the right test.

- **MAINT-001: the EC2 root volume is encrypted, in 7m45s rather than the 30-60 min estimated (August 21, 2026)** — The root volume was `Encrypted: false`, which was the weakest answer on the client security questionnaire ([SECURITY_AND_PRIVACY_POSTURE.md](docs/SECURITY_AND_PRIVACY_POSTURE.md) §0.2) **because uploaded files live on it** — including the prefixes that will hold passport scans and bank details. Swapped for `vol-08f22cd184c2bf880` (50 GB gp3, 3000/125, AES-256, `alias/aws/ebs`) following [EBS_ENCRYPTION_RUNBOOK.md](docs/EBS_ENCRYPTION_RUNBOOK.md); as-executed record, verification and rollback state in the new **[MAINTENANCE_LOG.md](docs/MAINTENANCE_LOG.md)** — a planned-change counterpart to INCIDENTS.md, separated because the useful questions differ (*what broke and how do we stop it* vs *did the change do what it claimed, is the rollback still open, what did the estimate get wrong*). **What made it safe is one property: nothing in the procedure modifies the original volume.** A snapshot is a read, the encrypted volume is a new object, the original is detached not erased — so at every step before cleanup, rollback was "reattach the disk you already have", ~5 min, which is a stronger position than any backup because the disk itself is sitting there intact. **Two estimates were wrong in opposite directions, and both are instructive.** The *downtime* estimate was 4-8× too pessimistic: enabling account-default EBS encryption removes the separate encrypted-copy pass entirely (`CreateVolume` from an *unencrypted* snapshot now yields an *encrypted* volume), so the runbook's copy step had already been deleted — **re-measure a plan after changing a default, because the cheapest step is often the one that stopped being necessary**. The *warm-up* estimate was 10× too optimistic: predicted "a minute or two", took **25 minutes**, because the box had deployed **six times that day** and each deploy pulls a Docker image onto the root volume. **On a box that deploys via `docker compose pull`, the root disk is one of the FASTEST-changing things in the system, not one of the slowest** — so the no-deploy rule between warm-up and window is load-bearing, not hygiene. The payoff was exact and measurable: **25 minutes of copying with the box UP, 35 seconds with it DOWN.** **Three judgement calls worth keeping:** (a) **AWS-managed key, not customer-managed** — the opposite of the recommendation for the document bucket, deliberately: a root volume encrypted with a CMK becomes **unbootable** if that key is ever disabled or its policy broken, so the blast radius of a key mistake is the whole server rather than one prefix; (b) **"skip OS shutdown" declined** — the entire reason to stop the instance is a *filesystem-consistent* snapshot, and that snapshot is what the new root is built from, so a forced stop trades the one property that makes the job safe for ~40 seconds (**force-stop is a recovery tool for an unresponsive box, never a time-saver on a healthy one**); (c) **a second concurrent snapshot would not have been faster** — EBS increments are computed against the last **completed** snapshot, so one started mid-flight inherits the same base and has identical blocks to ship. Also: EBS `Progress` is coarse and non-linear (0% for ten minutes, 36% for five, then a jump) — do not extrapolate from it. Verified after: encrypted volume at `/dev/sda1`, filesystem clean at 65%, **516 upload files** across all 7 prefixes, both containers healthy, crontab 45 lines, `/health` + `/worker/health` + uploads 200 and **private prefixes still 403** (checked deliberately — a disk swap is exactly the change that could restore an old `public/` tree under the allow-list). Elastic IP retained, so no DNS change. **Found during the window, not fixed:** for ~90 s every visitor got a bare `502 Bad Gateway / nginx/1.24.0 (Ubuntu)` — reads as broken rather than briefly-down, and discloses server + version; the fix is a static nginx page returned as **503 with `Retry-After`, not 200** (a 200 tells crawlers the page is genuinely that content and tells Uptime Robot the site is healthy while it is down), tracked in ROADMAP. **Outstanding and deliberately not done:** the old volume and **four** unencrypted snapshots are retained as the rollback for ~1 week — deleting them is the only irreversible step, and until then §0.2 is closed on the live system but not on every historical copy, which is what the posture doc now says.

- **ADMIN-gate sweep: `x-org-id` was a cross-tenant write, and a correct predicate that nobody called (August 21, 2026)** — Prompted by rehearsal finding 4 (Docs/Infra were `adminOnly`, written when ADMIN meant an MMG employee). The sweep asked one question of every authorisation check — *is this still right when ADMIN, or SUPER_ADMIN, is a customer?* — and **the serious finding was not ADMIN at all.** Six sites let a `SUPER_ADMIN` swap the acting organisation by setting an `x-org-id` request header, on the role alone with no `PLATFORM_ORG_ID` check: [api-auth.ts](src/lib/api-auth.ts) ×2 (session + mobile JWT, **inherited by 12 API routes**), [organization/route.ts](src/app/api/organization/route.ts) GET **and PUT** — the header's value went straight into `organization.update({ where: { id: orgId } })`, so it was a cross-tenant **write** — plus branding and the events list. **This is a worse shape than any of the five rehearsal defects, and the difference is the direction of failure.** Those all failed **closed**: no lane, RLS matches nothing, an empty screen. This fails **open** — the overridden id is used directly, so a later `runWithTenant(orgId)` enters the *target* tenant's lane and RLS serves their rows faithfully. **RLS is not a backstop against a caller who has been handed the wrong tenant id; it is an accomplice.** All six now resolve through one `resolveActingOrgId()` in [platform-operator.ts](src/lib/platform-operator.ts) (honoured only for a platform operator; honoured overrides log at **info** because a cross-tenant action must be traceable, refused ones at **warn** because reaching for another tenant is a security event, and the no-op case the org switcher produces routinely is silent so the warn stays meaningful). **Tier 2:** four platform-ops routes said `SUPER_ADMIN` and never called `denyNonOperator` — `api/logs` + `api/logs/archive` (cross-tenant `SystemLog`, DELETE-capable), `api/admin/alerts/silence` (silences **our** paging), `api/organizations` (enumerates every tenant). **Verified correct and deliberately unchanged:** every `organization/*` credential/user/branding route (a tenant admin managing their own org), `admin/infra` + `traffic` (the bare check is a coarse pre-filter;
